quietus.description: As celebrations of Daphne Oram's centenary culminate with an all-day celebration in Bradford, Claire Biddles speaks to a host of artists, from her contemporaries to previous Oram Award winners, to get a measure of her immense contribution to electronic music Photo © Daphne Oram Trust The pioneering work of Daphne Oram was not fully recognised until after her death in 2003 – but now, over 20 years later, she is rightly recognised as one of the most important electronic musicians of the 20th century. A co-founder of the BBC’s legendary Radiophonic Workshop in 1958, Oram was one of the first composers to use electronic sound in her work, and is known for her early use of electronic tape,…

quietus.description: Daryl Worthington considers the extent to which Spool’s Out offers investment advice, and reviews a crop of tapes including a footwork legend from Japan going ultra-crisp, mesmerising live code improvisations, ferocious eco-pop and more Roxanne Harris, photo by Cecilia Díaz Betz Five thousand dollars. That’s how much an original copy of Prince’s The Versace Experience on cassette could be worth, according to Finance Buzz, a website which offers “the resources and support necessary to navigate the complexities of personal finance”. That Prince tape, which contained previews of tracks from his then forthcoming The Gold Experience, was issued in 1995 and given to attendees at a fashion show…

quietus.title: Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia – Phren
quietus.description: Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia Phren Spooky sounds from two Italian masters of modern electro-acoustic composition Phren by Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia Marta Salogni and Stefano Pilia’s Phren is music of accretion. Inputs are fed through Pilia’s chain of filters and tape echo and on into Salogni’s Revox reel-to-reel tape machine for further manipulation and modulation, the signals absorbing new layers and mutations as they go. According to the release notes, that initial input is often Pilia’s guitar, but the pair’s plastic approach to sound makes that far from obvious. They telescope the act of mediation, mottling, shading and bending signals as they pass from sound source to ears.…

quietus.title: Remember Them: The Incalculable Legacy of Juan Atkins
quietus.description: Alex Maiolo salutes a visionary musician – "The Originator" of techno – who died on Saturday night Juan Atkins was born in Detroit, Michigan in 1962. His parents split when he was a teen. The plan was for him and his father to move to California, but his grandparents made the case for them to take up residence down the street in the Detroit suburb of Belleville. This was only the first time Juan’s grandmother, Lily, had a direct effect on the history of electronic music.The second was when she helped the 15-year-old buy a monosynth. Already playing in funk bands, Atkins took note of Bernie Worrell’s work in Funkadelic. Apparently Lily could absolutely tear it up on the Hammond B3...

quietus.title: A Form of Utopianism: Cluster’s Sowiesoso at 50
quietus.description: From avant garde beginnings to ambient endings, Cluster reconfigured rock music as much as Kraftwerk, says Toby Manning. In the late 70s and early 80s, British music took a distinctly European turn, from Bowie’s “Heroes” in 1977 to Ultravox’s ‘Vienna’ in 1981, peaking with Kraftwerk’s ‘The Model’ hitting UK no. 1 the following year. Whether it was the after-effects of the EEC referendum or a growing anti-Americanism in the wake of Watergate and Vietnam, this new Europeanism temporarily sidelined music’s traditional Transatlantic passage for the artier terrain over the Channel. Chart hits like Visage’s ‘Fade To Grey’ in 1980, The Passions’ 1981 ‘I’m In Love With A German Film Star’, or The…

quietus.title: How Pete Doherty’s Mega-Breakfast Predicted GB Music Radio
quietus.description: Pete Paphides reaches for the Gaviscon as he considers national identity, large plates of fried food, and what would be on the playlist were he celebrating British culture on the airwaves Pete Doherty eating his breakfast at the Dalby Cafe, via Instagram It’s been ten years since, over a Muswell Hill cuppa, my pop-loving compañero Bob Stanley floated a theory that was, on the face of things, a mite fanciful. Bob contended that those of us who wanted Britain to remain in the EU didn’t have a comparably snappy word to which we could align our...

quietus.title: The Last Path – Blunt Synopsis
quietus.description: The Last Path Blunt Synopsis Formerly known as Bad Amputee, trio from the north-east of England take things slow. Real slow Blunt Synopsis by The Last Path When the sort of music The Last Path play really lands, the secret to it doing so is in how it just teeters on the absolute precipice of unsalvageable dourness. Guitars that sound innately metallic, not as in the genre but evocative of a large amount of lead ingots plummeting from the sky onto rural limestone. Vocals that draw out nigh on every vowel sound, not for melismatic or otherwise showy reasons but just to figuratively look you in the eye and say, “I’ll finish singing this line when I’m ready, thanks”. Blunt Synopsis is the…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Steve Gunn :: Sundowner
aquariumdrunkard.description: A long neglected album dates to the beginning of Steve Gunn’s career, when it seemed that the guitarist might become a Takoma-style picker rather than the songwriter/improvisational experimenter he has since turned out to be. The playing is agile and folk-blues focused; the singing, when it comes, is similarly traditional and not as polished as Gunn has become. The music earned the approval of no less than Jack Rose, and its reels and rambles and psychedelic drones feel very much of a piece with the master’s work.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Chrome Chasm :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: The Houston-based trio known as Chrome Chasm features three veteran improvisers doing what they do best — improvising. Together, guitarist Tom Carter (Charalambides), saxophonist/flautist Mlee Marie (Hearts of Animals) and pedal steel-er Will Adams (Lower Dens, Ka-Nives) create bewitching, twilit music that’s somehow both minimalist and wide-open — a vast landscape that somehow contains countless sonic details. Aquarium Drunkard chatted with Tom, Mlee and Will to find out more.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Miles Davis: Europe ‘71
aquariumdrunkard.description: Across the Miles Davis electric era there’s no greater divide than that between 1972’s On the Corner and what came before it. But the signposts are there if you know where to look, with recordings from a European tour in the fall of ‘71 revealing Miles subtly, deftly moving the pieces into place for his next iteration.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Jason Dungan & Johan Carøe :: Routine
aquariumdrunkard.description: Copenhagen-based composers Jason Dungan (Blue Lake) and Johan Carøe join forces on Routine , a quietly transportive collection of ambient folk and new age soundscapes shaped through an exchange of musical fragments. Blending acoustic instrumentation, electronics, and Dungan’s self-designed 36-string zither, the duo arrive at something intimate and unhurried—a luminous meditation on domestic ritual, the rhythms of everyday life, and the quiet wonder of being alive.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Panamint :: S/T
aquariumdrunkard.description: Panamint began as a studio experiment between longtime collaborators Anna St. Louis and producer Jarvis Taveniere, who reunited to put Taveniere’s new Los Angeles studio through its paces. What started with left-field covers of Post Malone and Helene Smith soon evolved into a set of original recordings, joined by Danny Garcia, aka Reverend Baron. Out this week, their self-titled debut EP draws on the timeless pull of vintage soul and classic pop.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Sam Gendel :: Advanced White Trash
aquariumdrunkard.description: In his classic book Mythologies, French thinker Roland Barthes criticizes plastic because it can be molded into anything—cheap, colorful surfaces open to infinite transformation. Contemporary pop is made of the same stuff, and Sam Gendel’s Advanced White Trash makes the case for what’s beautiful, even freeing, about it. The record sounds like something that was uploaded to SoundCloud at 3 a.m., a Roland Sound Canvas emulator buffering on a dying phone someone found in a Walmart parking lot, and still it comes out strangely appealing, almost hypnotic.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Ana Palindrome :: A MAN A CURE

mubi.title: Can This Be Dixie?: Building the Hollywood South
mubi.description: Hallelujah (King Vidor, 1929). The American South exists only in the imagination, yet it’s as real as sin. It cannot merely be the land situated beneath the Mason-Dixon (the historical survey line that traditionally demarcated Northern and Southern states), whose citizens fought under the banner of the Confederacy; one cannot ignore the obviously Southern states of West Virginia and Kentucky, or the political split between West and East Tennessee. It cannot be a shared culture or a shared history, for the residents of Jacksonville, Florida, find little in common with those families tucked deep in the Appalachian hollers or those ruling the oil-rich cities of eastern Texas. It is not a…

The spirit of nostalgic celebration and victory lapping from 2025's "TIFFty" celebration had evaporated, leaving behind the gritty residue of cinema as a commercial product. Lacking the elegance of “Marché du Film” at Cannes and the specificity of “European Film Market” at Berlinale, for their new industry initiative TIFF settled on a name that evokes the absurdity of local hero Matt Johnson’s Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie (2025). Please show us!” “Are you mad? You could’ve been killed! If you want to die, I can arrange it.” — Born to Fight (Panna Rittikrai, 1984) For many martial arts movie fans in the mid-2000s, Tony Jaa was king. Sundry moments established his reign. He has worked with both established and emerging directors from Latin America and Europe, including Martín Rejtman, Teddy Williams, Affonso Uchoa, Konstantina Kotzamani, Ico Costa, and Thomas Woodroffe. His filmography is characterized by projects that embrace significant artistic risks and a strong authorial vision, helping to renew the paths of Latin American…

What happens when a veteran director who helped shape postwar German-language cinema in the 1950s and ’60s decides to have one more go at it in his later years? mubi.description: One Sings, the Other Doesn't (Agnès Varda, 1977). In her memoir, Varda par Agnès , the French director describes herself as “une féministe de terrain plus qu’une discuteuse,” roughly translated as “a feminist on the ground rather than in theory.” Later in the book, she describes the “feminists” discussing her work, implying that she was outside this group. How feminist she reads from any angle now is unclear. Many would, for instance, find her focus on the body and childbirth essentialist. Her 1975 short, Réponse de femmes: Notre corps, notre sexe ( Women Reply: Our Bodies, Our Sex ), opens with this prompt: “What does it mean to be a woman?” The text is painted on glass and held up by two…

A few months earlier, the same film had world premiered at Cannes, in the Un Certain Regard section, and walked away with a special mention for the Caméra d’Or. It was the first Nigerian film to be programmed in the official selection at the festival. Variety called Akinola Davies Jr.’s film miraculous. Rotten Tomatoes aggregated the critical assessment as 98% positive. However, there exists a cultural invisibility at home that stands against these genuine international recognitions.
